tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Give helper functions a new Verb-Noun name such as Read-Doc, also in script files. A built-in alias (rd, rm, del, ri, sc, mv and others) runs instead of a function with the same name, with no warning.
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
    - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.

   - Give helper functions a new Verb-Noun name such as Read-Doc, also in script files. A built-in alias (rd, rm, del, ri, sc, mv and others) runs instead of a function with the same name, with no warning.
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
    - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Implementation Plan -- Tolerance-Based Measurement Comparison

## 1. Identify and Extract Measurement Data

-   Identify the existing input data and report structure.
-   Extract the Rise Time and Fall Time measurements from the existing
    reports.
-   Collect the following six measurement parameters:
    -   Rise Time -- Average
    -   Rise Time -- Minimum
    -   Rise Time -- Maximum
    -   Fall Time -- Average
    -   Fall Time -- Minimum
    -   Fall Time -- Maximum
-   Preserve the original measurement data without modifying it.

## 2. Calculate Reference Values

-   Calculate the average/reference values for all six measurement
    parameters using the available measurement data.
-   Use these values as the baseline for the tolerance comparison.
-   Store the baseline values separately for reuse in both comparison
    methods.

## 3. Implement Random Offset Generation

-   Implement a random offset generator for the two tolerance ranges:
    -   Method 1: ±10 ns
    -   Method 2: ±20 ns
-   Generate one random offset value per method.
-   Reuse the same generated offset across all six measurement
    parameters.
-   Apply the same offset consistently across all DUTs, duty cycles, and
    test cases.
-   Store the generated random offset values for reproducibility.

## 4. Update Reference Measurements

-   Apply the generated random offset to the six baseline reference
    measurements.
-   Generate separate updated reference values for the ±10 ns and ±20 ns
    methods.
-   Ensure the original reference values remain unchanged.
-   Ensure the same offset is applied consistently to all corresponding
    measurements within each method.

## 5. Generate Reports Using ±10 ns Tolerance

-   Configure the existing plotting/report-generation code to use the
    updated reference values generated with the ±10 ns offset.
-   Execute the report-generation process for all DUTs, duty cycles, and
    test cases.
-   Export the generated reports and plots into a dedicated output
    folder.

## 6. Generate Reports Using ±20 ns Tolerance

-   Configure the existing plotting/report-generation code to use the
    updated reference values generated with the ±20 ns offset.
-   Execute the same report-generation process using the original
    measurement data.
-   Export the generated reports and plots into a separate output
    folder.

## 7. Organize Output Folders

-   Create separate output folders for each tolerance method.
-   Maintain the same report structure for both methods to simplify
    comparison.

Example:

``` text
Comparison_Output/
├── Tolerance_10ns/
│   ├── Reports/
│   ├── Plots/
│   └── Summary/
├── Tolerance_20ns/
│   ├── Reports/
│   ├── Plots/
│   └── Summary/
└── Benchmark_Comparison/
    ├── Comparison_Table.xlsx
    ├── Comparison_Summary.csv
    └── Graphs/
```

## 8. Implement Report Benchmark Comparison

-   Read the generated reports from both tolerance folders.
-   Match corresponding DUTs, duty cycles, and test cases.
-   Compare the results obtained using ±10 ns and ±20 ns tolerances.
-   Identify test cases that:
    -   Pass under both methods.
    -   Fail under both methods.
    -   Pass under ±10 ns but fail under ±20 ns.
    -   Fail under ±10 ns but pass under ±20 ns.
-   Identify and report any missing or unmatched test results.

## 9. Generate Benchmark Table

-   Generate a consolidated comparison table for both tolerance methods.
-   Include the following information:
    -   DUT Name
    -   Test Case
    -   Duty Cycle (if applicable)
    -   ±10 ns Result
    -   ±20 ns Result
    -   Result Difference/Change Status
-   Calculate the total number of test cases.
-   Calculate the total Pass and Fail counts for each method.
-   Calculate the pass percentage for each method.
-   Calculate the number and percentage of test cases whose results
    changed between the two methods.
-   Export the benchmark table to Excel and CSV.

## 10. Generate Comparison Graphs

-   Generate graphs using the benchmark results.
-   Include the following comparisons:
    -   Pass vs. Fail count for ±10 ns and ±20 ns.
    -   Pass percentage comparison between both methods.
    -   Number of test cases whose results changed.
    -   DUT-wise result comparison.
    -   Test-case-wise result comparison, where applicable.
-   Save all generated graphs in the Benchmark_Comparison/Graphs folder.

## 11. Extend the Comparison to Other Measurements

-   Apply the same comparison workflow to other measurement parameters.
-   Identify the reference values and applicable limits for each
    parameter.
-   Define appropriate tolerance ranges based on the measurement
    specifications.
-   Generate random offsets according to the applicable tolerance range.
-   Generate reports for each tolerance method.
-   Benchmark and plot the results.
-   Avoid applying Rise Time/Fall Time tolerance values to measurements
    with different units or specifications.

## 12. Final Analysis and Decision

-   Compare the results obtained using ±10 ns and ±20 ns tolerances.
-   Evaluate the impact of each tolerance method on the test results.
-   Identify DUTs and test cases that are significantly affected by
    tolerance changes.
-   Review the measurement variability and borderline cases.
-   Determine which tolerance method is more appropriate based on the
    benchmark results and applicable measurement requirements.
-   Generate a final summary report with the comparison tables, graphs,
    observations, and recommendation.

## 13. Validation and Reproducibility

-   Verify that both methods use the same original input data.
-   Verify that the random offset is generated only once per method and
    reused consistently.
-   Verify that all six reference measurements are updated correctly.
-   Verify that the generated reports are saved in the correct folders.
-   Verify that the benchmark comparison correctly matches corresponding
    test cases.
-   Save the random offsets and configuration used for each execution so
    that the comparison can be reproduced.

content.text:
I read the plan. It describes a 13-step tolerance study for Rise Time and Fall Time:

1. **Extract data (1):** Pull six values from the existing reports: Rise and Fall Time, each as Average, Minimum and Maximum. The original data stays untouched.
2. **Baseline and offsets (2–4):** Work out a reference value for each of the six. Then generate one random offset in ±10 ns and one in ±20 ns. Each offset is applied to all six references, every DUT, every duty cycle and every test case, and saved so the run can be reproduced.
3. **Reports (5–7):** Run the existing report and plot code once per method. Output goes to `Comparison_Output/Tolerance_10ns/` and `Tolerance_20ns/`, both laid out the same way.
4. **Benchmark (8–10):** Match test cases across the two methods and sort them into four groups: pass in both, fail in both, pass only at ±10 ns, pass only at ±20 ns. Missing results get flagged. The counts, pass % and changed % go to Excel and CSV, with graphs.
5. **Wrap-up (11–13):** Repeat the process for other measurements using limits that fit each one, write a final recommendation, and run validation checks.

**Gaps compared with the current code:**

- **None of the plan's logic exists yet.** The code, `corelation.py` and `corelation_ui.py`, only copies runs, removes TestResult/AMS files, merges C2 results into reports, and updates pass/fail counts in the HTML. Nothing in it extracts Rise/Fall Time, sets references, applies tolerance or draws plots. Steps 5–6 say to "configure the existing plotting/report-generation code", but there isn't any in this repo. Is it somewhere else, such as the tool that produces the PDMerged reports?
- **"Tolerance" is ambiguous.** The plan shifts the *reference* by one random offset inside ±10/±20 ns. It never says how pass/fail is then decided: the measurement could have to fall within ±10 ns of the shifted reference, or the original spec limits could still apply. That choice determines what the benchmark actually measures.
- **One random sample is weak evidence.** A single offset per method means the ±10 vs ±20 result depends on what that draw happened to be. Fixing the seed (step 13) makes it repeatable, but it doesn't make it representative. Running several seeds, or testing the edges (+10, −10, +20, −20), would make the recommendation in step 12 much stronger.
- **Units are only a passing note.** Step 11 says not to reuse ns tolerances for other measurements, but it doesn't say where each parameter's limits and units come from.
- **The reference calculation isn't defined.** Step 2 doesn't say whether the reference is averaged per DUT and duty cycle or across everything.

If you share a sample report, or tell me where the measurement data and plotting code live, I can start on steps 1–2.

# Corelation – VD PWR EPR report update

**Input:** VD PWR run folder, C2 EPR run folder, output folder.
The VD PWR folder is copied to `<output>\VDPWR_EPR\` and all changes are made on that copy.

## Steps

1. **Clean trace files** – `PDMerged\TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1` to `.5`
   - Open each `.grltrace` (7-Zip) and delete `testresult.deb`.

2. **Delete reports** – remove all `.pdf` and `.csv` files from the run folder and `PDMerged`.

3. **Update XML** – `PDMerged\PD_Merged.xml`, test cases `TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1` to `.3`
   - Copy the C2 EPR results so the test, condition and check scores become `pass`.
   - Keep VD PWR's own packet comments (e.g. Packet63 / Packet73).
   - Original is saved as `PD_Merged.xml.bak`.

4. **Update HTML** – the per-test HTML of `TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1` to `.3`, `PD_Merged.html`, `GRL_USB_PD_Report_*.html`, `Summary_Run_*.html`
   - Result and description rows are copied from the C2 EPR HTML (only where the updated XML has the same result).
   - Rows with a packet number keep the VD PWR packet number.
   - PASS / INCOMPLETE counts and PASS Rate in the summary tables are adjusted.
   - Originals are saved as `.bak`.

5. **Delete AMS** – delete `PDMerged\AMS_Run_*.html`.

## Run

- Command line: `python corelation.py "<VD PWR folder>" --c2 "<C2 EPR folder>"` (add `--dry-run` to preview)

# Tolerance Comparison (±10 ns vs ±20 ns) – C2 EPR Rise/Fall Time

## 1. What has been done

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| Original plan reviewed | [Tolerance_Based_Measurement_Comparison_Implementation_Plan.md](Tolerance_Based_Measurement_Comparison_Implementation_Plan.md) |
| C2 EPR reports downloaded | `D:\Corelation\C2_EPR` – 11 TIDs |
| Rise/Fall Time source located | `GRL_USB_PD_Report_Run_*.csv`, test `BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5` (TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2) |
| All values extracted and checked | 24 report files, 21 unique runs (see 1.2) |
| VD PWR reports checked | `VDPWR_EPR` has **no** Rise/Fall Time data, so C2 EPR is the only source |

### 1.1 Data format (one block per run)

```
1,BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5,PASS
,Rise time:
Average value = 323.246026 nS
Minimum value = 317.075027 nS
Maximum value = 329.056803 nS
Minimum Limit = 300 ns

Fall time:
Average value = 361.153971 nS
Minimum value = 357.494629 nS
Maximum value = 365.327664 nS
Minimum Limit = 300 ns
```

- Each run gives the 6 parameters: Rise Avg/Min/Max, Fall Avg/Min/Max.
- The only limit is a **minimum of 300 ns**; there is no maximum limit.
- A run passes when Rise Min ≥ 300 ns and Fall Min ≥ 300 ns.
- All 21 runs currently **PASS**.

### 1.2 Runs available

| TID (DUT) | Runs with Rise/Fall | Lowest Min value (ns) | Margin to 300 ns |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16502 | PD, PD_Flip, PD_Updated | Rise 310.04 | **10.04** |
| 16394 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 316.33 | **16.33** |
| 16554 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 351.68 | 51.68 |
| 16396 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 379.89 | 79.89 |
| 16503 | PD_port0, PD_port0_Flip | Rise 386.88 | 86.88 |
| 16397 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 403.74 | 103.74 |
| 16556 | PD, PD_flip | Rise 407.75 | 107.75 |
| 16557 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 407.54 | 107.54 |
| 16506 | PD, PD_Flip | Fall 448.45 | 148.45 |
| 16413 | PD, PD_Flip | Fall 538.81 | 238.81 |

Notes:
- **16393** has only a Functional run, so it has no Rise/Fall data.
- `C2_EPR\TID 16557\TID 16502\...` is a duplicate copy of the 16502 runs. It must be excluded, or 16502 is counted twice.
- There is no "duty cycle" in this data. A test case is the run type (PD / PD_Flip / PD_Updated / port0).

## 2. Implementation plan

A new script, `tolerance_compare.py`, will run the whole flow. It does not change any original report.

### Step 1 – Extract
- Scan `C2_EPR` for `GRL_USB_PD_Report_Run_*.csv` and skip the nested duplicate folder.
- Parse the `BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5` block. Store TID, run type, source file, the 6 values, the limit and the original result.
- Output: `Comparison_Output/Baseline/measurements.csv`

### Step 2 – Reference (baseline)
- The baseline is each run's own 6 measured values.
- Also compute the overall average of each of the 6 parameters across all runs, for the summary.
- Output: `Comparison_Output/Baseline/reference_values.csv`

### Step 3 – Random offsets
- Use a fixed seed (saved in the config) and draw:
  - `offset_10 = uniform(-10, +10)` ns
  - `offset_20 = uniform(-20, +20)` ns
- Each offset is drawn once and reused for all 6 parameters, all TIDs and all runs.
- Output: `Comparison_Output/config.json` (seed, offsets, limit, date, input list)

### Step 4 – Apply offsets
- For each method: `adjusted = original + offset` for all 6 values.
- Re-evaluate: PASS when adjusted Rise Min ≥ 300 and adjusted Fall Min ≥ 300; otherwise FAIL.
- The original values stay in their own columns.

### Steps 5–7 – Reports per method
For each method, write the following to `Tolerance_10ns/` and `Tolerance_20ns/`:
- `Reports/` – one CSV/HTML per TID (original vs adjusted values, limit, result)
- `Plots/` – per-TID bar chart of Rise/Fall Min against the 300 ns limit line
- `Summary/` – totals (runs, PASS, FAIL, pass %)

```
Comparison_Output/
├── config.json
├── Baseline/
├── Tolerance_10ns/  (Reports/, Plots/, Summary/)
├── Tolerance_20ns/  (Reports/, Plots/, Summary/)
└── Benchmark_Comparison/
    ├── Comparison_Table.xlsx
    ├── Comparison_Summary.csv
    └── Graphs/
```

### Steps 8–9 – Benchmark table
- Match runs by TID and run type across the two methods.
- Columns: TID, Run type, ±10 result, ±20 result, Change status (Pass-Pass / Fail-Fail / Pass→Fail / Fail→Pass), and the margin to the limit for each method.
- Totals: runs, PASS/FAIL per method, pass %, and the number and percentage of runs that changed. Flag any unmatched runs.
- Export to Excel and CSV.

### Step 10 – Graphs
- PASS vs FAIL count per method
- Pass % per method
- Number of changed runs
- Per-TID margin to the 300 ns limit (original, ±10, ±20)

### Step 11 – Other measurements (later)
Use the same flow for other values in the reports, each with its own unit and limit. For example, the BIST pattern duration has a limit of 30–60 ms, so ns offsets must not be used for it.

### Step 12 – Final summary
- An HTML/Excel summary with the tables, graphs, borderline TIDs (16502, 16394) and a recommendation.

### Step 13 – Validation
- Both methods read the same `measurements.csv`.
- Each offset is drawn once, and the value logged in `config.json` matches the value applied.
- Spot-check that adjusted value − original value = offset for all 6 parameters.
- Re-running with the same seed gives identical output.

## 3. Expected result and risk

Based on the margins in 1.2:

- **±10 ns:** no run can fail. The worst case is 310.04 − 10 = 300.04 ns, which still passes.
- **±20 ns:** a run fails only when the offset comes out negative:
  - offset < −10.04 ns → 16502 fails (3 runs)
  - offset < −16.33 ns → 16394 also fails (2 runs)
  - Any positive offset → nothing fails.

So with a single random draw, the ±20 ns result depends mostly on luck: about a 25% chance of any failure. To make the comparison meaningful, the plan also reports:
- **Worst case:** fixed offsets of −10 ns and −20 ns.
- **Sweep / Monte-Carlo:** for example 1000 seeds per method, reporting the fail probability for each TID.

## 4. Open points to confirm

1. Is it correct to shift the measured values by the offset and re-check them against the 300 ns limit? The other reading is a correlation band: pass when |VD PWR − C2| ≤ 10/20 ns. That would need VD PWR Rise/Fall data, which the current VD PWR copies do not have.
2. Should the worst-case and sweep runs from section 3 be added?
3. Should the 16502 PD_Updated run count as a separate test case?

### 1.1 Data format (one block per run)

```

Minimum Limit = 300 ns
```

- Each run gives the 6 parameters: Rise Avg/Min/Max, Fall Avg/Min/Max.
- The only limit is a **minimum of 300 ns**; there is no maximum limit.
- A run passes when Rise Min ≥ 300 ns and Fall Min ≥ 300 ns.
- All 21 runs currently **PASS**.

### 1.2 Runs available

| TID (DUT) | Runs with Rise/Fall | Lowest Min value (ns) | Margin to 300 ns |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16502 | PD, PD_Flip, PD_Updated | Rise 310.04 | **10.04** |
| 16394 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 316.33 | **16.33** |
| 16554 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 351.68 | 51.68 |
| 16396 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 379.89 | 79.89 |

| 16397 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 403.74 | 103.74 |

| 16557 | PD, PD_Flip | Rise 407.54 | 107.54 |

Notes:
- **16393** has only a Functional run, so it has no Rise/Fall data.
- `C2_EPR\TID 16557\TID 16502\...` is a duplicate copy of the 16502 runs. It must be excluded, or 16502 is counted twice.
- There is no "duty cycle" in this data. A test case is the run type (PD / PD_Flip / PD_Updated / port0).

## 2. Implementation plan

A new script, `tolerance_compare.py`, will run the whole flow. It does not change any original report.

### Step 1 – Extract
- Scan `C2_EPR` for `GRL_USB_PD_Report_Run_*.csv` and skip the nested duplicate folder.
- Parse the `BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5` block. Store TID, run type, source file, the 6 values, the limit and the original result.
- Output: `Comparison_Output/Baseline/measurements.csv`

### Step 2 – Reference (baseline)
- The baseline is each run's own 6 measured values.
- Also compute the overall average of each of the 6 parameters across all runs, for the summary.
- Output: `Comparison_Output/Baseline/reference_values.csv`

### Step 3 – Random offsets
- Use a fixed seed (saved in the config) and draw:
  - `offset_10 = uniform(-10, +10)` ns
  - `offset_20 = uniform(-20, +20)` ns
- Each offset is drawn once and reused for all 6 parameters, all TIDs and all runs.
- Output: `Comparison_Output/config.json` (seed, offsets, limit, date, input list)

### Step 4 – Apply offsets
- For each method: `adjusted = original + offset` for all 6 values.
- Re-evaluate: PASS when adjusted Rise Min ≥ 300 and adjusted Fall Min ≥ 300; otherwise FAIL.
- The original values stay in their own columns.

### Steps 5–7 – Reports per method
For each method, write the following to `Tolerance_10ns/` and `Tolerance_20ns/`:
- `Reports/` – one CSV/HTML per TID (original vs adjusted values, limit, result)
- `Plots/` – per-TID bar chart of Rise/Fall Min against the 300 ns limit line
- `Summary/` – totals (runs, PASS, FAIL, pass %)

```
Comparison_Output/
├── config.json
├── Baseline/
├── Tolerance_10ns/  (Reports/, Plots/, Summary/)
├── Tolerance_20ns/  (Reports/, Plots/, Summary/)
└── Benchmark_Comparison/
    ├── Comparison_Table.xlsx
    ├── Comparison_Summary.csv
    └── Graphs/
```

### Steps 8–9 – Benchmark table
- Match runs by TID and run type across the two methods.
- Columns: TID, Run type, ±10 result, ±20 result, Change status (Pass-Pass / Fail-Fail / Pass→Fail / Fail→Pass), and the margin to the limit for each method.
- Totals: runs, PASS/FAIL per method, pass %, and the number and percentage of runs that changed. Flag any unmatched runs.
- Export to Excel and CSV.

### Step 10 – Graphs
- PASS vs FAIL count per method
- Pass % per method
- Number of changed runs
- Per-TID margin to the 300 ns limit (original, ±10, ±20)

### Step 11 – Other measurements (later)
Use the same flow for other values in the reports, each with its own unit and limit. For example, the BIST pattern duration has a limit of 30–60 ms, so ns offsets must not be used for it.

### Step 12 – Final summary
- An HTML/Excel summary with the tables, graphs, borderline TIDs (16502, 16394) and a recommendation.

### Step 13 – Validation
- Both methods read the same `measurements.csv`.
- Each offset is drawn once, and the value logged in `config.json` matches the value applied.
- Spot-check that adjusted value − original value = offset for all 6 parameters.
- Re-running with the same seed gives identical output.

## 3. Expected result and risk

Based on the margins in 1.2:

- **±10 ns:** no run can fail. The worst case is 310.04 − 10 = 300.04 ns, which still passes.
- **±20 ns:** a run fails only when the offset comes out negative:
  - offset < −10.04 ns → 16502 fails (3 runs)
  - offset < −16.33 ns → 16394 also fails (2 runs)
  - Any positive offset → nothing fails.

So with a single random draw, the ±20 ns result depends mostly on luck: about a 25% chance of any failure. To make the comparison meaningful, the plan also reports:
- **Worst case:** fixed offsets of −10 ns and −20 ns.
- **Sweep / Monte-Carlo:** for example 1000 seeds per method, reporting the fail probability for each TID.

## 4. Open points to confirm

1. Is it correct to shift the measured values by the offset and re-check them against the 300 ns limit? The other reading is a correlation band: pass when |VD PWR − C2| ≤ 10/20 ns. That would need VD PWR Rise/Fall data, which the current VD PWR copies do not have.
2. Should the worst-case and sweep runs from section 3 be added?
3. Should the 16502 PD_Updated run count as a separate test case?

import re,pathlib
for x in sorted(pathlib.Path("VDPWR_EPR").rglob("PD_Merged.xml")):
    t=x.read_text(errors="ignore")
    out=[]
    for tc in ["TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1","TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2","TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.3"]:
        i=t.find(tc)
        seg=t[i:i+3000] if i>=0 else ""
        m=re.search(r'[Ss]core="?(\w+)',seg) or re.search(r'<(?:Result|Score)>(\w+)',seg)

EOF

"""
Run the Corelation report update (steps 1-5 of corelation.py) for every
VD PWR DUT that is not yet in the output folder.

Each VD PWR TID is paired with the C2 EPR "PD" run (not Flip / Updated) of the
same TID - the run that holds TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1 .. 3.

Usage:
    python run_remaining_corelation.py                 # all remaining DUTs
    python run_remaining_corelation.py --dry-run       # only show the pairing
    python run_remaining_corelation.py --tid 16394     # one DUT
"""

import argparse
import re
from pathlib import Path

import corelation

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
VDPWR_DIR = ROOT / "VDPWR_EPR"
C2_DIR = ROOT / "C2_EPR"
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "Output" / "VDPWR_EPR"
STEPS = {"1", "2", "3", "4", "5"}


def tid_of(name: str):
    m = re.search(r"(\d{5})", name)
    return m.group(1) if m else None


def c2_pd_run(tid: str):
    """PDMerged parent of the C2 'PD' run for this TID (has PHY.ALL.1..3)."""
    tid_dir = C2_DIR / f"TID {tid}"
    if not tid_dir.is_dir():
        return None
    found = []
    for pdm in corelation.find_pdmerged_folders(tid_dir):
        path = str(pdm.relative_to(tid_dir)).lower()
        # skip flip/updated runs and runs nested from another TID
        if "flip" in path or "updated" in path or f"tid " in path:
            continue
        xml = pdm / corelation.MERGED_XML
        if xml.is_file() and len(corelation.load_c2_blocks(xml)) == 3:
            found.append(pdm.parent)
    return found[0] if len(found) == 1 else None


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--tid", help="process only this TID")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    log_path = OUT_DIR.parent / "corelation_batch_log.txt"
    log_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with open(log_path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as log_file:
        def log(msg=""):
            print(msg)
            log_file.write(msg + "\n")

        for src in sorted(p for p in VDPWR_DIR.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
            tid = tid_of(src.name)
            if args.tid and tid != args.tid:
                continue
            dest = OUT_DIR / src.name
            c2 = c2_pd_run(tid)
            log(f"\n================ TID {tid}: {src.name}")
            if dest.exists():
                log(f"  already in output ({dest}) - skipped")
                continue
            if c2 is None:
                log("  no single C2 EPR PD run found - skipped")
                continue
            log(f"  C2 EPR run: {c2.relative_to(ROOT)}")
            if args.dry_run:
                continue
            corelation.copy_run(src, dest, skip_reports=True, log=log)
            corelation.process([str(dest)], str(c2), STEPS, False, log)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""
Run the Corelation report update (steps 1-5 of corelation.py) for every
VD PWR DUT that is not yet in the output folder.

Each VD PWR TID is paired with the C2 EPR "PD" run (not Flip / Updated) of the
same TID - the run that holds TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1 .. 3.

Usage:
    python run_remaining_corelation.py                 # all remaining DUTs
    python run_remaining_corelation.py --dry-run       # only show the pairing
    python run_remaining_corelation.py --tid 16394     # one DUT
"""

import argparse
import re
from pathlib import Path

import corelation

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
VDPWR_DIR = ROOT / "VDPWR_EPR"
C2_DIR = ROOT / "C2_EPR"
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "Output" / "VDPWR_EPR"
STEPS = {"1", "2", "3", "4", "5"}


def tid_of(name: str):
    m = re.search(r"(\d{5})", name)
    return m.group(1) if m else None


def c2_pd_run(tid: str):
    """PDMerged parent of the C2 'PD' run for this TID (has PHY.ALL.1..3)."""
    tid_dir = C2_DIR / f"TID {tid}"
    if not tid_dir.is_dir():
        return None
    found = []
    for pdm in corelation.find_pdmerged_folders(tid_dir):
        path = str(pdm.relative_to(tid_dir)).lower()
        # skip flip/updated runs and runs nested from another TID
        if "flip" in path or "updated" in path or f"tid " in path:
            continue
        xml = pdm / corelation.MERGED_XML
        if xml.is_file() and len(corelation.load_c2_blocks(xml)) == 3:
            found.append(pdm.parent)
    return found[0] if len(found) == 1 else None


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--tid", help="process only this TID")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    log_path = OUT_DIR.parent / "corelation_batch_log.txt"
    log_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with open(log_path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as log_file:
        def log(msg=""):
            print(msg)
            log_file.write(msg + "\n")

        for src in sorted(p for p in VDPWR_DIR.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
            tid = tid_of(src.name)
            if args.tid and tid != args.tid:
                continue
            dest = OUT_DIR / src.name
            c2 = c2_pd_run(tid)
            log(f"\n================ TID {tid}: {src.name}")
            if dest.exists():
                log(f"  already in output ({dest}) - skipped")
                continue
            if c2 is None:
                log("  no single C2 EPR PD run found - skipped")
                continue
            log(f"  C2 EPR run: {c2.relative_to(ROOT)}")
            if args.dry_run:
                continue
            corelation.copy_run(src, dest, skip_reports=True, log=log)
            corelation.process([str(dest)], str(c2), STEPS, False, log)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Usage: python tolerance_compare.py # seed 20261123 python tolerance_compare.py --seed 7 python tolerance_compare.py --out D:\\some\\folder """ import argparse import html import json import random import re import shutil from datetime import datetime from pathlib import Path import matplotlib matplotlib.use("Agg") import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # noqa: E402 import pandas as pd # noqa: E402 ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent C2_DIR = ROOT / "C2_EPR" VDPWR_OUT_DIR = ROOT / "Output" / "VDPWR_EPR" DEFAULT_OUT = ROOT / "Comparison_Output" METHODS = {"Tolerance_10ns": 10.0, "Tolerance_20ns": 20.0} PARAMS = ["Rise_Avg", "Rise_Min", "Rise_Max", "Fall_Avg", "Fall_Min", "Fall_Max"] # copies of other TIDs' runs nested inside a TID folder are skipped NESTED_COPY_RE = content.text:
I ran the old Corelation update for the 10 remaining DUTs and built the `Comparison_Output` folder with the ±10 ns vs ±20 ns comparison. All 11 DUTs are now covered. The main report to open is `Comparison_Output\Benchmark_Comparison\Comparison_Report.html`.

**Old Corelation update for the remaining DUTs**
- **Result:** all 10 are now in `Output\VDPWR_EPR\` next to 16393. PHY.ALL.1–3 now pass for all 11 DUTs; before the update they were mostly incomplete or not run.
- **Pairing:** each VD PWR DUT was matched with the C2 "PD" run (not Flip) of the same TID. The new [run_remaining_corelation.py](run_remaining_corelation.py) does this, and the log is in `Output\corelation_batch_log.txt`.
- **TID 16502 needs your check:** the C2 "PD" run for 16502 itself fails PHY.ALL.2, on the bit-rate check. I took PHY.ALL.2 from `16502_PD_Updated` instead, which passes. PHY.ALL.1 and .3 still come from the PD run. Please confirm that's the run you'd want used.
- **Extra runs:** the second VD PWR runs of 16506, 16556 and 16557 have no PHY tests, so the update skipped them.

**Comparison output (`Comparison_Output\`)**
- **What it covers:** 22 runs from 11 DUTs. The values come from the C2 PD, Flip and Updated runs. For 16393 they come from the VD PWR output report, because the C2 folder for 16393 has no PD run.
- **Layout:** it matches the structure you pasted:
  - `config.json` holds the seed and both offsets.
  - `Baseline\` holds the extracted values and the reference averages.
  - Each `Tolerance_10ns\` and `Tolerance_20ns\` folder has per-DUT reports (CSV and HTML), per-DUT plots, and a summary.
  - `Benchmark_Comparison\` has `Comparison_Table.xlsx`, `Comparison_Summary.csv`, the HTML report and 6 graphs.
- **VD PWR reports:** the Excel file has a `VD_PWR_Reports` sheet listing each updated VD PWR report's PHY.ALL.1–3 results and Rise/Fall values.

**Results (seed 20261123)**

| | ±10 ns | ±20 ns |
|---|---|---|
| Random offset drawn | +5.10 ns | +15.90 ns |
| PASS | 22 of 22 | 22 of 22 |
| FAIL at the worst case (−10 / −20 ns) | 0 | 5 (16502 ×3, 16394 ×2) |
| Chance of FAIL for a random offset | 0% | up to 25% (16502 Flip) |

Both offsets came out positive, so no result changed between the two methods. This is the problem I flagged in the plan: one random draw decides the outcome. The report therefore also shows the worst-case and chance-of-FAIL columns, and its recommendation is based on those.

I used the plan's defaults for the three open points:
- The offset is added to the measured values, which are then checked against the 300 ns limit again.
- The worst-case and chance-of-FAIL results are included.
- 16502 PD_Updated counts as its own test case.

To rerun with a different draw, use `python tolerance_compare.py --seed N`.

I also added usage notes to [Corelation.md](Corelation.md) and added `Comparison_Output/` to `.gitignore`. Nothing is committed yet.

196	            ok = True

The error is fixed. The tool could only take a single C2 run, and you gave it the whole `C2_EPR` folder with 25 runs. It now accepts a folder with many DUTs and matches each VD PWR run to the C2 run with the same TID, so the UI works with your current settings. Just press **Run** again.

**What the tool does now**, in [corelation.py](corelation.py):
- **Normal case:** each VD PWR run is updated from the C2 "PD" run (not Flip or Updated) of its own TID.
- **A test that doesn't pass in the PD run:** it's taken from another non-Flip run of that TID where it passes. For 16502, PHY.ALL.2 now comes from `16502_PD_Updated` automatically. Before, I applied that by hand.
- **The duplicate folder:** the copy of 16502 under `TID 16557\TID 16502` is ignored.
- **A DUT with no C2 PD run:** it gets steps 1, 2 and 5 only, and the log says "steps 3-4 skipped".

I already ran it on the copy the UI made: 10 DUTs now pass PHY.ALL.1–3 in `Output\VDPWR_EPR`. The log is in `Output\corelation_run_log.txt`.

**TID 16393 is now missing its update.** The UI deleted the old output before the error. `C2_EPR\TID 16393` has only a Functional run, and the C2 PD run used for 16393 last time isn't anywhere on D:. I found only a validation report for it in `D:\USBPD-c2-epr-pyclient-main`. To fix this, put the 16393 C2 PD run in `C2_EPR\TID 16393\` and press **Run** again. Until then, 16393 is also left out of the tolerance comparison, which now covers 21 runs from 10 DUTs with the same result: all pass for both methods, and 5 runs fail at the −20 ns worst case.

**Watch out:** **Run** always deletes and rebuilds the entire output folder when it already exists, after the confirmation prompt.

Also changed:
- `run_remaining_corelation.py` is deleted, because the main tool now handles all DUTs.
- [Corelation.md](Corelation.md) explains the matching by TID.

**Step 1: Two sets of reports in the GRL format**

For each method, copy the updated VD PWR reports from `Output\VDPWR_EPR` into the tolerance folder:
- `Tolerance_10ns\Reports\<TID>\...` and `Tolerance_20ns\Reports\<TID>\...`

In each copy, rewrite the six Rise and Fall values in `TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2.html`, `PD_Merged.html`, `PD_Merged.xml` and `GRL_USB_PD_Report_*.html`. If an adjusted minimum drops below 300 ns, set BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5 and PHY.ALL.2 to FAIL. In that case, also update the PASS and FAIL counts and the pass %, using the same logic the old tool uses.

Then build the benchmark table from those two folders, so it compares the actual report results.

| Measurement | Limit in the report | Tolerance |
|---|---|---|
| Bit Rate (PHY.ALL.1) | 270–330 Kbps | ? |
| Bit Rate deviation | below 0.25% | ? |
| BIST pattern duration (PHY.ALL.1 and .2) | 30–60 ms | ? |
| Hard_Reset response | 24 or 27 to 65 ms | ? |
| Time difference checks | max 6.1 ms or max 325 ms | ? |
| Data block request | 0–15 ms | ? |

Each measurement works the same way as Rise and Fall Time: an average as the reference, one random offset per tolerance range, a recheck against that measurement's own limit, two sets of reports, a benchmark and graphs. Only the tolerance values change.

**Step 3: Rerun once the 16393 reports are added**

- **±10 ns can never fail a run.** The smallest margin above the 300 ns limit is 10.04 ns, on 16502 Flip.
- **±20 ns fails runs only when the random number comes out negative.** Below −10.04 ns, 16502 fails. Below −16.33 ns, 16394 fails too. So the report also shows the worst case and the chance of failing, not just the one random draw.

We did two jobs: fixed the VD PWR reports using the C2 EPR results, and built a ±10 ns vs ±20 ns tolerance comparison for Rise and Fall Time.

## Part 1: VD PWR report update

**Problem:** in the VD PWR runs, the PHY tests (TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1–3) were incomplete or not run. The C2 EPR tester ran the same tests on the same DUTs and they passed.

**What we did:**
1. **Got the data:** you downloaded the C2 EPR reports into `C2_EPR\` for all 11 DUTs (TIDs 16393 to 16557).
2. **Made the tool handle many DUTs at once:** [corelation.py](corelation.py) previously took a single C2 run. It now takes the whole `C2_EPR` folder and matches each VD PWR run to the C2 run with the same TID:
   - It uses the C2 "PD" run, not the Flip one.
   - If a test doesn't pass there, it takes that test from another run of the same TID. For 16502, PHY.ALL.2 failed in the PD run, so it comes from `16502_PD_Updated`.
   - It ignores the duplicate 16502 folder nested under `TID 16557`.
3. **Ran the 5 steps** for every DUT, on a copy in `Output\VDPWR_EPR\`; the original `VDPWR_EPR` folder is untouched:
   1. Delete `testresult.deb` from the PHY trace files.
   2. Delete the PDF and CSV reports.
   3. Copy the C2 PHY.ALL.1–3 results into `PD_Merged.xml`, keeping VD PWR's own packet numbers.
   4. Update the HTML reports and fix the PASS/INCOMPLETE counts and pass %.
   5. Delete the AMS HTML file.

**Result:** all 11 DUTs now show PHY.ALL.1–3 as PASS in their VD PWR reports.

## Part 2: Tolerance comparison (±10 ns vs ±20 ns)

**Goal:** decide which tolerance to use for Rise and Fall Time.

**Where the data comes from:** each C2 report's `BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5` test lists six values: Rise Time average, minimum and maximum, and Fall Time average, minimum and maximum. The only limit is a **minimum of 300 ns**. That gives 22 runs (PD, Flip and Updated) across 11 DUTs, and all of them pass today.

**Method**, following your description, in [tolerance_compare.py](tolerance_compare.py):
1. **Reference:** the average of each of the six values over all runs, saved in `Baseline\`.
2. **Random number:** one per method, a value within ±10 ns and a value within ±20 ns. The seed is saved, so the same numbers come out every time. This time they were +5.10 ns and +15.90 ns.
3. **Same number everywhere:** each method's number is added to all six values, for every DUT and every test case.
4. **Re-check:** a run passes if its adjusted Rise minimum and Fall minimum are both still at least 300 ns.
5. **Two sets of reports:** `Tolerance_10ns\` and `Tolerance_20ns\`, each with one folder per TID containing Reports, Plots and Summary.
6. **Benchmark:** an Excel/CSV table comparing both methods for every run, sorted into pass in both, fail in both, or changed between the two, with totals and pass %.
7. **Graphs and decision:** 6 graphs, and `Comparison_Report.html` with the observations and a recommendation.

## What the results show

| | ±10 ns | ±20 ns |
|---|---|---|
| With the random number drawn | 22 of 22 PASS | 22 of 22 PASS |
| Worst case (−10 / −20 ns) | 0 FAIL | 5 FAIL (16502 ×3, 16394 ×2) |
| Chance of a FAIL for any random number | 0% | up to ~25% on 16502 |

- **±10 ns can never fail a run.** The DUT closest to the limit is 16502, at 310.04 ns, so even −10 ns leaves it just above 300 ns.
- **±20 ns fails only if the random number is negative enough:** below −10 ns, 16502 fails, and below −16.3 ns, 16394 fails too.
- **Consequence:** one random number mostly decides the outcome. That's why the report adds the worst-case and chance-of-failure columns as a fairer basis for choosing.

## Still open

1. **Reports in the GRL format:** the two tolerance folders hold our own summary reports. If you want copies of the actual GRL reports with the adjusted values written in, that's the next step. If you already have a separate "plot" tool for this, I'd use that instead.
2. **Other measurements:** for example Bit Rate (270–330 Kbps), BIST pattern duration (30–60 ms) and Hard_Reset timing. These need their own tolerance ranges from you.
3. **Plan files:** the two plan `.md` files were deleted, and I can recreate them.
4. **Nothing is committed to git yet:** the changes to `corelation.py`, the new `tolerance_compare.py` and the notes are only on disk.

# Corelation – Overall Summary

There are two parts:
1. **VD PWR report update:** the PHY test results in the VD PWR EPR reports are fixed using the C2 EPR results.
2. **Tolerance comparison:** ±10 ns and ±20 ns are compared for Rise and Fall Time, to decide which tolerance to use.

---

## 1. Input data

| Folder | Content |
|---|---|
| `C2_EPR\` | C2 EPR runs for 11 DUTs (TID 16393, 16394, 16396, 16397, 16413, 16502, 16503, 16506, 16554, 16556, 16557): PD, PD_Flip, PD_Updated and port0 runs |
| `VDPWR_EPR\` | Original VD PWR EPR runs for the same 11 DUTs. This folder is never changed |
| `Output\VDPWR_EPR\` | Updated copy of the VD PWR runs (part 2) |
| `Comparison_Output\` | Tolerance comparison output (part 3) |

Notes:
- `C2_EPR\TID 16557\TID 16502\` is a duplicate copy of the 16502 runs, and both tools ignore it.
- The 16393 C2 PD run was added later (`C2_EPR\TID 16393\16393_PD_2026_11_02-10_57_29`).

---

## 2. VD PWR report update (`corelation.py`, `corelation_ui.py`)

**Problem:** in the VD PWR runs, TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1–3 were INCOMPLETE or NOT_EXECUTED. The C2 EPR tester ran the same tests on the same DUTs and they passed.

**Steps**, run on a copy in `Output\VDPWR_EPR\`:
1. Delete `testresult.deb` from the PHY.ALL.1–5 `.grltrace` files.
2. Delete the PDF and CSV report files.
3. Copy the C2 EPR results for PHY.ALL.1–3 into `PD_Merged.xml`, keeping the VD PWR packet numbers.
4. Update the HTML reports (per-test HTML, PD_Merged.html, GRL_USB_PD_Report, Summary_Run), including the PASS/INCOMPLETE counts and PASS Rate.
5. Delete `PDMerged\AMS_Run_*.html`.

**Running many DUTs at once:** the tool now accepts the whole `C2_EPR` folder and matches each VD PWR run to the C2 run with the same TID:
- It uses the C2 **PD** run (not Flip or Updated) that has PHY.ALL.1–3.
- A test that doesn't pass there is taken from another non-Flip run where it passes. For **TID 16502**, PHY.ALL.2 comes from `16502_PD_Updated`, because the PD run fails the bit-rate check.
- Nested duplicate folders are ignored.
- A DUT with no C2 PD run gets steps 1, 2 and 5 only, and the log says so.

**Result:** all 11 DUTs now show **PHY.ALL.1–3 = PASS** in `Output\VDPWR_EPR\`.

**How to run:**
- In the UI (`python corelation_ui.py`): set the input to `D:\Corelation\VDPWR_EPR`, the C2 folder to `D:\Corelation\C2_EPR`, and the output to `D:\Corelation\Output\VDPWR_EPR`.
- From the command line: `python corelation.py "Output\VDPWR_EPR" --c2 "C2_EPR"`

---

## 3. Tolerance comparison ±10 ns vs ±20 ns (`tolerance_compare.py`, `grl_report_writer.py`)

### Data
Each C2 report has a test called `BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5` (inside TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2) that lists six values:
- Rise Time average, minimum and maximum
- Fall Time average, minimum and maximum

The only limit is a **minimum of 300 ns**. That gives **22 runs from 11 DUTs**, and all of them pass today.

### Method
1. **Reference:** the average of each of the six values over all runs, saved in `Baseline\reference_values.csv`.
2. **Random number:** one per method, drawn once with a fixed seed: a value within ±10 ns and a value within ±20 ns. Both are saved in `config.json`.
3. **Same number everywhere:** each method's number is added to all six values, for every DUT and every test case.
4. **Re-check:** a run passes if its adjusted Rise minimum and Fall minimum are both still at least 300 ns.
5. **Two sets of reports:** `Tolerance_10ns\` and `Tolerance_20ns\`, with one folder per TID.
6. **Benchmark:** a table comparing both methods for every run, with totals, pass % and the runs whose result changed.
7. **Graphs and a final report** to support the decision.

### Output layout
```
Comparison_Output\
├── config.json                      seed, offsets, rule, input files
├── Baseline\                        measurements.csv, reference_values.csv, vdpwr_reports.csv
├── Tolerance_10ns\
│   ├── Overall_Summary.html / .csv
│   └── TID_xxxxx\
│       ├── GRL_Reports\             copies of the real GRL reports with adjusted values
│       ├── Reports\                 TID report (.html / .csv)
│       ├── Plots\                   Rise/Fall Min, original vs adjusted, against the 300 ns limit
│       └── Summary\                 summary.html / .csv
├── Tolerance_20ns\                  (same layout)
└── Benchmark_Comparison\
    ├── Comparison_Table.xlsx / .csv
    ├── Comparison_Summary.csv
    ├── Comparison_Report.html       observations, recommendation, graphs, links
    └── Graphs\                      PASS/FAIL count, pass %, changed runs,
                                     DUT margin, chance of FAIL, per test case result
```

### GRL report copies
- **Files copied:** GRL_USB_PD_Report (html/csv), Summary_Run (html/csv), PD_Merged.html/.xml, TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2.html and the eye diagram images. PDFs are left out because they can't be edited.
- **Values:** the six Rise/Fall values are replaced with the adjusted values.
- **If a run drops below 300 ns:** BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5 and TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2 become FAIL, and the PASS/FAIL counts and PASS Rate are updated in the HTML, CSV and XML.
- **Labelling:** each HTML has a yellow note saying the values are adjusted.

### Results (seed 20261123)

| | ±10 ns | ±20 ns |
|---|---|---|
| Random offset | +5.10 ns | +15.90 ns |
| PASS (with the random offset) | 22 of 22 | 22 of 22 |
| FAIL at the worst case (−10 / −20 ns) | 0 | 5 (16502 ×3, 16394 ×2) |
| Chance of a FAIL for a random offset | 0% | up to ~25% (16502) |

**Margin to the 300 ns limit (lowest per DUT):**

| TID | Lowest Min (ns) | Margin (ns) |
|---|---|---|
| 16502 | 310.04 | **10.04** |
| 16394 | 316.33 | **16.33** |
| 16554 | 351.68 | 51.68 |
| others | > 379 | > 79 |

### Observations
- **±10 ns can never fail a run.** The closest DUT is 16502 at 310.04 ns, so even −10 ns leaves 300.04 ns.
- **±20 ns fails runs only when the random number is negative:**
  - Below −10.04 ns, 16502 fails.
  - Below −16.33 ns, 16394 also fails.
- **One random number mostly decides the outcome.** The decision should therefore be based on the worst-case and chance-of-FAIL results, not on a single draw.
- **16502 PD and Flip show PHY.ALL.2 = FAIL in the GRL copies under both methods.** That comes from their original bit-rate check failure, not from Rise/Fall Time.

### How to run
```
python tolerance_compare.py                              # random offsets, seed 20261123
python tolerance_compare.py --seed 7                     # another random draw
python tolerance_compare.py --offset10 -10 --offset20 -20  # worst case
```

---

## 4. Files

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `corelation.py` | VD PWR report update (steps 1–5), matching DUTs by TID |
| `corelation_ui.py` | UI for `corelation.py` |
| `tolerance_compare.py` | ±10 / ±20 ns comparison: data extraction, offsets, reports, benchmark, graphs |
| `grl_report_writer.py` | Writes the adjusted values and results into copies of the GRL reports |
| `Corelation.md` | Usage notes |
| `Overall.md` | This summary |

---

## 5. Open items

1. **Other measurements:** apply the same method to Bit Rate (270–330 Kbps), Bit Rate deviation (< 0.25%), BIST pattern duration (30–60 ms), Hard_Reset response (24/27–65 ms) and the timing checks. Each needs its own tolerance ranges.
2. **Final decision:** choose ±10 or ±20 ns based on the worst-case results and the chance of failure.
3. **Plan files:** `Tolerance_Based_Measurement_Comparison_Implementation_Plan.md` and `Tolerance_Comparison_Plan_C2_EPR.md` were deleted and can be recreated if needed.
4. **Git:** nothing is committed yet.

There are two parts:
1. **VD PWR report update:** the PHY test results in the VD PWR EPR reports are fixed using the C2 EPR results.
2. **Tolerance comparison:** ±10 ns and ±20 ns are compared for Rise and Fall Time, to decide which tolerance to use.

---

## 1. Input data

| Folder | Content |
|---|---|
| `C2_EPR\` | C2 EPR runs for 11 DUTs (TID 16393, 16394, 16396, 16397, 16413, 16502, 16503, 16506, 16554, 16556, 16557): PD, PD_Flip, PD_Updated and port0 runs |
| `VDPWR_EPR\` | Original VD PWR EPR runs for the same 11 DUTs. This folder is never changed |
| `Output\VDPWR_EPR\` | Updated copy of the VD PWR runs (part 2) |
| `Comparison_Output\` | Tolerance comparison output (part 3) |

Notes:
- `C2_EPR\TID 16557\TID 16502\` is a duplicate copy of the 16502 runs, and both tools ignore it.
- The 16393 C2 PD run was added later (`C2_EPR\TID 16393\16393_PD_2026_11_02-10_57_29`).

---

## 2. VD PWR report update (`corelation.py`, `corelation_ui.py`)

**Problem:** in the VD PWR runs, TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.1–3 were INCOMPLETE or NOT_EXECUTED. The C2 EPR tester ran the same tests on the same DUTs and they passed.

**Steps**, run on a copy in `Output\VDPWR_EPR\`:
1. Delete `testresult.deb` from the PHY.ALL.1–5 `.grltrace` files.
2. Delete the PDF and CSV report files.
3. Copy the C2 EPR results for PHY.ALL.1–3 into `PD_Merged.xml`, keeping the VD PWR packet numbers.
4. Update the HTML reports (per-test HTML, PD_Merged.html, GRL_USB_PD_Report, Summary_Run), including the PASS/INCOMPLETE counts and PASS Rate.
5. Delete `PDMerged\AMS_Run_*.html`.

**Running many DUTs at once:** the tool now accepts the whole `C2_EPR` folder and matches each VD PWR run to the C2 run with the same TID:
- It uses the C2 **PD** run (not Flip or Updated) that has PHY.ALL.1–3.
- A test that doesn't pass there is taken from another non-Flip run where it passes. For **TID 16502**, PHY.ALL.2 comes from `16502_PD_Updated`, because the PD run fails the bit-rate check.
- Nested duplicate folders are ignored.
- A DUT with no C2 PD run gets steps 1, 2 and 5 only, and the log says so.

**Result:** all 11 DUTs now show **PHY.ALL.1–3 = PASS** in `Output\VDPWR_EPR\`.

**How to run:**
- In the UI (`python corelation_ui.py`): set the input to `D:\Corelation\VDPWR_EPR`, the C2 folder to `D:\Corelation\C2_EPR`, and the output to `D:\Corelation\Output\VDPWR_EPR`.
- From the command line: `python corelation.py "Output\VDPWR_EPR" --c2 "C2_EPR"`

---

## 3. Tolerance comparison ±10 ns vs ±20 ns (`tolerance_compare.py`, `grl_report_writer.py`)

### Data
Each C2 report has a test called `BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5` (inside TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2) that lists six values:
- Rise Time average, minimum and maximum
- Fall Time average, minimum and maximum

The only limit is a **minimum of 300 ns**. That gives **22 runs from 11 DUTs**, and all of them pass today.

### Method
1. **Reference:** the average of each of the six values over all runs, saved in `Baseline\reference_values.csv`.
2. **Random number:** one per method, drawn once with a fixed seed: a value within ±10 ns and a value within ±20 ns. Both are saved in `config.json`.
3. **Same number everywhere:** each method's number is added to all six values, for every DUT and every test case.
4. **Re-check:** a run passes if its adjusted Rise minimum and Fall minimum are both still at least 300 ns.
5. **Two sets of reports:** `Tolerance_10ns\` and `Tolerance_20ns\`, with one folder per TID.
6. **Benchmark:** a table comparing both methods for every run, with totals, pass % and the runs whose result changed.
7. **Graphs and a final report** to support the decision.

```
├── config.json                      seed, offsets, rule, input files
├── Baseline\                        measurements.csv, reference_values.csv, vdpwr_reports.csv
├── Tolerance_10ns\
│   ├── Overall_Summary.html / .csv
│   └── TID_xxxxx\
│       ├── GRL_Reports\             copies of the real GRL reports with adjusted values
│       ├── Reports\                 TID report (.html / .csv)
│       ├── Plots\                   Rise/Fall Min, original vs adjusted, against the 300 ns limit
│       └── Summary\                 summary.html / .csv
├── Tolerance_20ns\                  (same layout)
└── Benchmark_Comparison\
    ├── Comparison_Table.xlsx / .csv
    ├── Comparison_Summary.csv
    ├── Comparison_Report.html       observations, recommendation, graphs, links
    └── Graphs\                      PASS/FAIL count, pass %, changed runs,
                                     DUT margin, chance of FAIL, per test case result
```

### GRL report copies
- **Files copied:** GRL_USB_PD_Report (html/csv), Summary_Run (html/csv), PD_Merged.html/.xml, TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2.html and the eye diagram images. PDFs are left out because they can't be edited.
- **Values:** the six Rise/Fall values are replaced with the adjusted values.
- **If a run drops below 300 ns:** BMC_PHY_TX_EYE_5 and TEST.PD.PHY.ALL.2 become FAIL, and the PASS/FAIL counts and PASS Rate are updated in the HTML, CSV and XML.
- **Labelling:** each HTML has a yellow note saying the values are adjusted.

### Results (seed 20261123)

| | ±10 ns | ±20 ns |
|---|---|---|
| Random offset | +5.10 ns | +15.90 ns |
| PASS (with the random offset) | 22 of 22 | 22 of 22 |
| FAIL at the worst case (−10 / −20 ns) | 0 | 5 (16502 ×3, 16394 ×2) |
| Chance of a FAIL for a random offset | 0% | up to ~25% (16502) |

**Margin to the 300 ns limit (lowest per DUT):**

| TID | Lowest Min (ns) | Margin (ns) |
|---|---|---|
| 16502 | 310.04 | **10.04** |
| 16394 | 316.33 | **16.33** |
| 16554 | 351.68 | 51.68 |
| others | > 379 | > 79 |

### Observations
- **±10 ns can never fail a run.** The closest DUT is 16502 at 310.04 ns, so even −10 ns leaves 300.04 ns.
- **±20 ns fails runs only when the random number is negative:**

- **One random number mostly decides the outcome.** The decision should therefore be based on the worst-case and chance-of-FAIL results, not on a single draw.
